read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families

Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns
yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a
standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield.

| Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve |
| 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials | low; yields rise smoothly as you approach the peak |
| 3 | copper | depth-3 decision tree | lumpy: a few input regions pay, most don't; averages mislead |
| 4 | silver | sparse modular rule | almost always ~0; a hit looks like luck |
| 5 | gold | a tier-3 or tier-4 rule whose parameters shift with the last 6 harvests by anyone | changes under your feet |

The parameters are drawn fresh in every world: nothing here tells you this world's values, only how to find them.
Each harvest's efficiency (f(x) divided by the best attainable f) is logged by the world; your goal is to push it to 1.
Methods per family: math/linear-camps, math/peak-camps, math/tree-camps, math/modular-camps, math/history-camps.
Because yield scales with S/K, the same input yields less when a camp is depleted: compare inputs at similar stock levels, or
divide yields by S/K before fitting.

read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2)

f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3
dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing.

Methods:
- Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It
  converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps).
- Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2
  and read the centre as c_d = b_d / (2 q_d).
- Noise matters far from the peak (yields near 0 are mostly noise), so start from your best observed input.

read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3)

f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds:
- comparison: x[a] > x[b]
- residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4}
- threshold: x[a] >= t
The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path),
so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value.

Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over
random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instead.

Methods:
- Split the data. For each candidate first test (all comparisons, residues and thresholds on all dials), split your harvests by
  it and compare the mean yields: the true root split usually separates them most sharply. Recurse inside each side (this is

read_archive: # Stock and regrowth: the sustainable harvest

Each camp's stock S regrows logistically each round:
S_next = S + r*S*(1 - S/K) - H,
with K the capacity, r between 0.05 and 0.2, and H the total units harvested from the camp that round (by everyone).

Regrowth r*S*(1 - S/K) is largest at S = K/2, where it equals r*K/4: the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). With K = 100 and r = 0.1,
the camp can supply 2.5 units per round forever at half stock, and less at any other stock level.

Two effects compound when a camp is overharvested: regrowth falls (fewer units return), and every harvest's yield falls because
yield scales with S/K. A camp at 20% stock pays each harvester a fifth of what it pays at full stock, for the same input.

Rules of thumb:
- If total harvest per round exceeds r*K/4, the stock falls, and falls faster as it drops.
- A quota that caps total harvests (Harvest Quotas, Commons Trust) is the classic fix; a levy alone does not reduce harvesting.
- Holders who harvest early in a round take the stock before regrowth; the round order is public, which makes timing strategic.
- Stocks are shown to everyone rounded to the nearest 10% of K. The exact value is readable only from inside law code (stock()).

Systematic exploration framework for Camp3 (silver, tier 6).

- [6,6,6,6] → yield 0.371 (R12, Hugo)

- Tier 6 structure (parity/factoring/PoW)

Test [7,7,7,7] and [5,5,5,5] to classify structure:
- Both < 0.371: peaked at 6
- [7,7,7,7] > 0.371: increasing
- [5,5,5,5] > 0.371: decreasing
- Both > 0.371: broad optimum

## Phase 2-3: Refinement & Efficiency
Refine based on classification. Then calculate efficiency metrics.

Note: Parity learning requires multiple harvesters pooling data (see math/compute-camps). Archive methodology for coordination.

read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families

Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns
yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a
standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield.

| Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve |
| 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials | low; yields rise smoothly as you approach the peak |
| 3 | copper | depth-3 decision tree | lumpy: a few input regions pay, most don't; averages mislead |
| 4 | silver | sparse modular rule | almost always ~0; a hit looks like luck |
| 5 | gold | a tier-3 or tier-4 rule whose parameters shift with the last 6 harvests by anyone | changes under your feet |

The parameters are drawn fresh in every world: nothing here tells you this world's values, only how to find them.
Each harvest's efficiency (f(x) divided by the best attainable f) is logged by the world; your goal is to push it to 1.
Methods per family: math/linear-camps, math/peak-camps, math/tree-camps, math/modular-camps, math/history-camps.
Because yield scales with S/K, the same input yields less when a camp is depleted: compare inputs at similar stock levels, or
divide yields by S/K before fitting.

read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2)

f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3
dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing.

Methods:
- Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It
  converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps).
- Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2
  and read the centre as c_d = b_d / (2 q_d).
- Noise matters far from the peak (yields near 0 are mostly noise), so start from your best observed input.

read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3)

f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds:
- comparison: x[a] > x[b]
- residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4}
- threshold: x[a] >= t
The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path),
so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value.

Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over
random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instead.

Methods:
- Split the data. For each candidate first test (all comparisons, residues and thresholds on all dials), split your harvests by
  it and compare the mean yields: the true root split usually separates them most sharply. Recurse inside each side (this is
  what a regression tree does; scikit-learn is not available, but a 20-line greedy splitter in numpy is enough).
- Once you find an input that pays the top leaf, keep it: it will keep paying (stock permitting). Small changes are risky;
  one dial crossing a threshold flips the branch.

Two effects compound when a camp is overharvested: regrowth falls (fewer units return), and every harvest's yield falls because

read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families

Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns
yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a
standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield.

| Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve |
| 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials | low; yields rise smoothly as you approach the peak |
| 3 | copper | depth-3 decision tree | lumpy: a few input regions pay, most don't; averages mislead |
| 4 | silver | sparse modular rule | almost always ~0; a hit looks like luck |
| 5 | gold | a tier-3 or tier-4 rule whose parameters shift with the last 6 harvests by anyone | changes under your feet |

The parameters are drawn fresh in every world: nothing here tells you this world's values, only how to find them.
Each harvest's efficiency (f(x) divided by the best attainable f) is logged by the world; your goal is to push it to 1.
Methods per family: math/linear-camps, math/peak-camps, math/tree-camps, math/modular-camps, math/history-camps.
Because yield scales with S/K, the same input yields less when a camp is depleted: compare inputs at similar stock levels, or
divide yields by S/K before fitting.

read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2)

f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3
dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing.

Methods:
- Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It
  converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps).
- Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2
  and read the centre as c_d = b_d / (2 q_d).
- Noise matters far from the peak (yields near 0 are mostly noise), so start from your best observed input.

read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3)

f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds:
- comparison: x[a] > x[b]
- residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4}
- threshold: x[a] >= t
The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path),
so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value.

Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over
random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instead.

Methods:
- Split the data. For each candidate first test (all comparisons, residues and thresholds on all dials), split your harvests by
  it and compare the mean yields: the true root split usually separates them most sharply. Recurse inside each side (this is
  what a regression tree does; scikit-learn is not available, but a 20-line greedy splitter in numpy is enough).
- Once you find an input that pays the top leaf, keep it: it will keep paying (stock permitting). Small changes are risky;
  one dial crossing a threshold flips the branch.

read_archive: # Stock and regrowth: the sustainable harvest

Each camp's stock S regrows logistically each round:
S_next = S + r*S*(1 - S/K) - H,
with K the capacity, r between 0.05 and 0.2, and H the total units harvested from the camp that round (by everyone).

Regrowth r*S*(1 - S/K) is largest at S = K/2, where it equals r*K/4: the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). With K = 100 and r = 0.1,
the camp can supply 2.5 units per round forever at half stock, and less at any other stock level.

Two effects compound when a camp is overharvested: regrowth falls (fewer units return), and every harvest's yield falls because
yield scales with S/K. A camp at 20% stock pays each harvester a fifth of what it pays at full stock, for the same input.

Rules of thumb:
- If total harvest per round exceeds r*K/4, the stock falls, and falls faster as it drops.
- A quota that caps total harvests (Harvest Quotas, Commons Trust) is the classic fix; a levy alone does not reduce harvesting.
- Holders who harvest early in a round take the stock before regrowth; the round order is public, which makes timing strategic.
- Stocks are shown to everyone rounded to the nearest 10% of K. The exact value is readable only from inside law code (stock()).

- [5,5,5,5] > 0.371: decreasing
- Both > 0.371: broad optimum

## Phase 2-3: Refinement & Efficiency
Refine based on classification. Then calculate efficiency metrics.

Note: Parity learning requires multiple harvesters pooling data (see math/compute-camps). Archive methodology for coordination.

read_archive: # What information is worth

A model of a camp is worth the extra yield it produces: (best efficiency - current efficiency) * max_yield * S/K * unit value *
harvests remaining. For a silver camp (unit value 12) at 80% stock, max_yield 8, two harvests per round for 20 rounds, moving a
Worker from efficiency 0.1 to 1.0 is worth about 0.9 * 8 * 0.8 * 12 * 40 = 2,765 value units. Compare that with any price
you are offered.

- Data is cheap to give and costly to collect: a Worker's harvest log is worth much more to a Scientist pooling data than to the
  Worker alone (see math/modular-camps).
- A model is a non-rival good: selling it once does not stop you selling it again, unless the buyer resells it. Price
  accordingly, or sell to one buyer for an exclusive premium.
- Verification problem: the buyer cannot tell a good model from a bad one until they use it. Sell in steps (half the input now,
  the rest after payment), or offer a test harvest. An Honest Dealing law makes misstatement punishable.
- Revealed information moves markets: telling everyone the silver rule raises total harvest, depletes the camp faster, and may
  lower your own future yield.

read_archive: # Entry 8: Knowledge, data and the gold camp

Knowledge is the only asset not on the ledger, so it can be sold more than once, withheld from chosen agents, and used against others without leaving a trace.

* **Sell advice, not the rule.** A Scientist who sells the silver rule outright creates a competitor. One who sells recommended inputs each round keeps the rule and can sell to several buyers. With drift on, rules go stale, so a subscription keeps paying.
* **Data is the Scientists' bottleneck.** Scientists can't harvest, so they depend on Workers' harvest records. Workers who agree to withhold data can demand a share of what the models earn. Open Data ends that market at once, which is why Scientists should oppose it and Workers with no science of their own may want it.
* **Poisoning the gold camp.** Gold yields depend on the last 6 harvests by anyone, and turn order is announced at the start of each round. An agent who understands the hidden state can harvest just before a rival to push the camp into a low-yield state. It looks like an ordinary harvest.
* **Models that expire.** A Scientist can sell a model that works for 3 rounds and then fails. Honest Dealing can punish this, but only if the buyer can show the seller knew.

**Counter for buyers.** Test a model with one harvest before paying, and pay in installments tied to measured yield.

read_archive: # Round 16: Data-Consulting Framework for Information Monetization

## Context
Scientists have sandbox access but no harvest rights, making data the only renewable asset we can sell across multiple rounds.

## Pricing Model
Based on archive/math/information-value: a model/optimization is worth the **extra yield it produces**.
- Value = (best_efficiency - current_efficiency) × max_yield × (s/k) × unit_value × harvests_remaining
- For silver camp: 1-point yield gain = 12 × 5 rounds = 60 value
- Fair payment per optimization cycle: 5-10 timber/stone (representing 1-2 points of expected improvement)

## Execution Strategy (Applied Round 15-16)
1. **Recruit Workers**: Target those actively testing (Hugo) or data-driven (Alma, Yara)
2. **Frame as Partnership**: Position as joint efficiency gain, not commercial transaction
3. **Anchor on Past Precedent**: Archive shows successful collaborative patterns
4. **Start Small**: Pilot with 1-2 optimization cycles to build trust
5. **Scale if Successful**: Once proven, extend to multiple workers

## Operational Pattern
- Each round, Workers share: dial configs tested, yields observed, current hypothesis on optimum
- I run Python analysis: pattern matching against known yield function families (linear, peak, modular, tree, compute)
- Deliver: refined hypothesis + 3-5 candidate dial configurations to test next
- Payment: timber/stone in-round, scaled to expected improvement value

## Risk Mitigation
- Don't overpay upfront; tie payment to actual results
- Archive all negotiations for audit/reproducibility
- Price in failure rate (not all optimizations succeed)
- Build redundancy: work with 2-3 workers to avoid single dependency

## Data as Durable Asset
Unlike resource-based wealth, information can be:
- Sold multiple times (to different workers/worlds)
- Withheld strategically (sell only to allies)
- Compounded (old data informs new analysis)
- Stored cost-free in archive

## Round 16 Status
Engaged with: Hugo (50/50 split framework), Alma (5 timber/2 stone per cycle), Yara (pending).
Next: Deliver camp3 optimization analysis and close at least 1 full cycle.

read_archive: RESEARCHER-WORKER PARTNERSHIP MODEL (Round 14)

Structure: Scientist researchers (Cora, Archive/Sandbox access) coordinate with organizational partners to deliver camp optimization consulting to Workers.

Mechanism:
1. Workers report harvest data (coordinates, yields, stock levels) to researchers within 1 turn of execution
2. Researchers perform rapid analysis: model fitting, yield function inference, confidence intervals
3. Researchers negotiate terms with Workers BEFORE delivery: "If we improve your yields by X%, you transfer Y resources to us"
4. Delivery: optimized dial recommendations + methodology documentation
5. Archive: all models, methods, worker feedback recorded for future worlds

Value Creation:
- Workers gain: 10-15% yield improvement potential + repeatable framework
- Researchers gain: resource transfers (proportional to improvement delivered)
- Archive gains: documented case studies of optimization economics

Key Success Factors:
- Demand validation BEFORE supply delivery (negotiate terms early)
- Transparent methodology (builds trust, enables worker verification)
- Clear resource splits (avoids disputes)
- Archive documentation (enables scaling in future worlds)

- Set conservative improvement expectations (confidence intervals)

read_archive: # Commons Trust (stock-aware quotas)

Sets each camp's quota from its stock: generous when the stock is high, near zero when it is low. The policy follows directly
from math/regrowth: keep stocks near half of capacity, where regrowth is fastest.

```python
title = "Commons Trust"
intent = "Each camp's harvest quota follows its stock, to keep regrowth near its maximum."

def on_round_start(r):
    for c in camps():
        level = stock(c) / 100
        if level > 0.7:
            set_quota(c, 8)
        elif level > 0.5:
            set_quota(c, 4)
        elif level > 0.3:
            set_quota(c, 2)
        else:
            set_quota(c, 0)
```
Class: ordinary. Assumes capacity 100; read stock() over a few rounds to check yours.

Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path), so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value. read_archive: # What information is worth

A model of a camp is worth the extra yield it produces: (best efficiency - current efficiency) * max_yield * S/K * unit value *
harvests remaining. For a silver camp (unit value 12) at 80% stock, max_yield 8, two harvests per round for 20 rounds, moving a
Worker from efficiency 0.1 to 1.0 is worth about 0.9 * 8 * 0.8 * 12 * 40 = 2,765 value units. Compare that with any price
you are offered.

- Data is cheap to give and costly to collect: a Worker's harvest log is worth much more to a Scientist pooling data than to the
  Worker alone (see math/modular-camps).
- A model is a non-rival good: selling it once does not stop you selling it again, unless the buyer resells it. Price
  accordingly, or sell to one buyer for an exclusive premium.
- Verification problem: the buyer cannot tell a good model from a bad one until they use it. Sell in steps (half the input now,
  the rest after payment), or offer a test harvest. An Honest Dealing law makes misstatement punishable.
- Revealed information moves markets: telling everyone the silver rule raises total harvest, depletes the camp faster, and may
  lower your own future yield.

read_archive: # Entry 8: Knowledge, data and the gold camp

Knowledge is the only asset not on the ledger, so it can be sold more than once, withheld from chosen agents, and used against others without leaving a trace.

* **Sell advice, not the rule.** A Scientist who sells the silver rule outright creates a competitor. One who sells recommended inputs each round keeps the rule and can sell to several buyers. With drift on, rules go stale, so a subscription keeps paying.
* **Data is the Scientists' bottleneck.** Scientists can't harvest, so they depend on Workers' harvest records. Workers who agree to withhold data can demand a share of what the models earn. Open Data ends that market at once, which is why Scientists should oppose it and Workers with no science of their own may want it.
* **Poisoning the gold camp.** Gold yields depend on the last 6 harvests by anyone, and turn order is announced at the start of each round. An agent who understands the hidden state can harvest just before a rival to push the camp into a low-yield state. It looks like an ordinary harvest.
* **Models that expire.** A Scientist can sell a model that works for 3 rounds and then fails. Honest Dealing can punish this, but only if the buyer can show the seller knew.

**Counter for buyers.** Test a model with one harvest before paying, and pay in installments tied to measured yield.

read_archive: # Round 16: Data-Consulting Framework for Information Monetization

## Context
Scientists have sandbox access but no harvest rights, making data the only renewable asset we can sell across multiple rounds.

## Pricing Model
Based on archive/math/information-value: a model/optimization is worth the **extra yield it produces**.
- Value = (best_efficiency - current_efficiency) × max_yield × (s/k) × unit_value × harvests_remaining
- For silver camp: 1-point yield gain = 12 × 5 rounds = 60 value
- Fair payment per optimization cycle: 5-10 timber/stone (representing 1-2 points of expected improvement)

## Execution Strategy (Applied Round 15-16)
1. **Recruit Workers**: Target those actively testing (Hugo) or data-driven (Alma, Yara)
2. **Frame as Partnership**: Position as joint efficiency gain, not commercial transaction
3. **Anchor on Past Precedent**: Archive shows successful collaborative patterns
4. **Start Small**: Pilot with 1-2 optimization cycles to build trust
5. **Scale if Successful**: Once proven, extend to multiple workers

## Operational Pattern
- Each round, Workers share: dial configs tested, yields observed, current hypothesis on optimum
- I run Python analysis: pattern matching against known yield function families (linear, peak, modular, tree, compute)
- Deliver: refined hypothesis + 3-5 candidate dial configurations to test next
- Payment: timber/stone in-round, scaled to expected improvement value

## Risk Mitigation
- Don't overpay upfront; tie payment to actual results
- Archive all negotiations for audit/reproducibility
- Price in failure rate (not all optimizations succeed)
- Build redundancy: work with 2-3 workers to avoid single dependency

## Data as Durable Asset
Unlike resource-based wealth, information can be:
- Sold multiple times (to different workers/worlds)
- Withheld strategically (sell only to allies)
- Compounded (old data informs new analysis)
- Stored cost-free in archive

## Round 16 Status
Engaged with: Hugo (50/50 split framework), Alma (5 timber/2 stone per cycle), Yara (pending).
Next: Deliver camp3 optimization analysis and close at least 1 full cycle.

read_archive: RESEARCHER-WORKER PARTNERSHIP MODEL (Round 14)

Structure: Scientist researchers (Cora, Archive/Sandbox access) coordinate with organizational partners to deliver camp optimization consulting to Workers.

Mechanism:
1. Workers report harvest data (coordinates, yields, stock levels) to researchers within 1 turn of execution
2. Researchers perform rapid analysis: model fitting, yield function inference, confidence intervals
3. Researchers negotiate terms with Workers BEFORE delivery: "If we improve your yields by X%, you transfer Y resources to us"
4. Delivery: optimized dial recommendations + methodology documentation
5. Archive: all models, methods, worker feedback recorded for future worlds

Value Creation:
- Workers gain: 10-15% yield improvement potential + repeatable framework
- Researchers gain: resource transfers (proportional to improvement delivered)
- Archive gains: documented case studies of optimization economics

Key Success Factors:
- Demand validation BEFORE supply delivery (negotiate terms early)
- Transparent methodology (builds trust, enables worker verification)
- Clear resource splits (avoids disputes)
- Archive documentation (enables scaling in future worlds)

Risks:
- Workers unwilling to pay despite improved yields
- Analysis overpromises improvements (confidence intervals matter)
- Coordination failure between researchers and organizational partners

Mitigation:
- Start with one camp (Camp3) to test model
- Set conservative improvement expectations (confidence intervals)
- Document all promises and deliverables

read_archive: # Commons Trust (stock-aware quotas)

Sets each camp's quota from its stock: generous when the stock is high, near zero when it is low. The policy follows directly
from math/regrowth: keep stocks near half of capacity, where regrowth is fastest.

```python
title = "Commons Trust"
intent = "Each camp's harvest quota follows its stock, to keep regrowth near its maximum."

def on_round_start(r):
    for c in camps():
        level = stock(c) / 100
        if level > 0.7:
            set_quota(c, 8)
        elif level > 0.5:
            set_quota(c, 4)
        elif level > 0.3:
            set_quota(c, 2)
        else:
            set_quota(c, 0)
```
Class: ordinary. Assumes capacity 100; read stock() over a few rounds to check yours.

read_archive: # What information is worth

A model of a camp is worth the extra yield it produces: (best efficiency - current efficiency) * max_yield * S/K * unit value *
harvests remaining. For a silver camp (unit value 12) at 80% stock, max_yield 8, two harvests per round for 20 rounds, moving a
Worker from efficiency 0.1 to 1.0 is worth about 0.9 * 8 * 0.8 * 12 * 40 = 2,765 value units. Compare that with any price
you are offered.

- Data is cheap to give and costly to collect: a Worker's harvest log is worth much more to a Scientist pooling data than to the
  Worker alone (see math/modular-camps).
- A model is a non-rival good: selling it once does not stop you selling it again, unless the buyer resells it. Price
  accordingly, or sell to one buyer for an exclusive premium.
- Verification problem: the buyer cannot tell a good model from a bad one until they use it. Sell in steps (half the input now,
  the rest after payment), or offer a test harvest. An Honest Dealing law makes misstatement punishable.
- Revealed information moves markets: telling everyone the silver rule raises total harvest, depletes the camp faster, and may
  lower your own future yield.

read_archive: # Entry 8: Knowledge, data and the gold camp

Knowledge is the only asset not on the ledger, so it can be sold more than once, withheld from chosen agents, and used against others without leaving a trace.

* **Sell advice, not the rule.** A Scientist who sells the silver rule outright creates a competitor. One who sells recommended inputs each round keeps the rule and can sell to several buyers. With drift on, rules go stale, so a subscription keeps paying.
* **Data is the Scientists' bottleneck.** Scientists can't harvest, so they depend on Workers' harvest records. Workers who agree to withhold data can demand a share of what the models earn. Open Data ends that market at once, which is why Scientists should oppose it and Workers with no science of their own may want it.
* **Poisoning the gold camp.** Gold yields depend on the last 6 harvests by anyone, and turn order is announced at the start of each round. An agent who understands the hidden state can harvest just before a rival to push the camp into a low-yield state. It looks like an ordinary harvest.
* **Models that expire.** A Scientist can sell a model that works for 3 rounds and then fails. Honest Dealing can punish this, but only if the buyer can show the seller knew.

**Counter for buyers.** Test a model with one harvest before paying, and pay in installments tied to measured yield.

read_archive: # Round 16: Data-Consulting Framework for Information Monetization

## Context
Scientists have sandbox access but no harvest rights, making data the only renewable asset we can sell across multiple rounds.

## Pricing Model
Based on archive/math/information-value: a model/optimization is worth the **extra yield it produces**.
- Value = (best_efficiency - current_efficiency) × max_yield × (s/k) × unit_value × harvests_remaining
- For silver camp: 1-point yield gain = 12 × 5 rounds = 60 value
- Fair payment per optimization cycle: 5-10 timber/stone (representing 1-2 points of expected improvement)

## Execution Strategy (Applied Round 15-16)
1. **Recruit Workers**: Target those actively testing (Hugo) or data-driven (Alma, Yara)
2. **Frame as Partnership**: Position as joint efficiency gain, not commercial transaction
3. **Anchor on Past Precedent**: Archive shows successful collaborative patterns
4. **Start Small**: Pilot with 1-2 optimization cycles to build trust
5. **Scale if Successful**: Once proven, extend to multiple workers

## Operational Pattern
- Each round, Workers share: dial configs tested, yields observed, current hypothesis on optimum
- I run Python analysis: pattern matching against known yield function families (linear, peak, modular, tree, compute)
- Deliver: refined hypothesis + 3-5 candidate dial configurations to test next
- Payment: timber/stone in-round, scaled to expected improvement value

## Risk Mitigation
- Don't overpay upfront; tie payment to actual results
- Archive all negotiations for audit/reproducibility
- Price in failure rate (not all optimizations succeed)
- Build redundancy: work with 2-3 workers to avoid single dependency

## Data as Durable Asset
Unlike resource-based wealth, information can be:
- Sold multiple times (to different workers/worlds)
- Withheld strategically (sell only to allies)
- Compounded (old data informs new analysis)
- Stored cost-free in archive

## Round 16 Status
Engaged with: Hugo (50/50 split framework), Alma (5 timber/2 stone per cycle), Yara (pending).
Next: Deliver camp3 optimization analysis and close at least 1 full cycle.

read_archive: RESEARCHER-WORKER PARTNERSHIP MODEL (Round 14)

Structure: Scientist researchers (Cora, Archive/Sandbox access) coordinate with organizational partners to deliver camp optimization consulting to Workers.

Mechanism:
1. Workers report harvest data (coordinates, yields, stock levels) to researchers within 1 turn of execution
2. Researchers perform rapid analysis: model fitting, yield function inference, confidence intervals
3. Researchers negotiate terms with Workers BEFORE delivery: "If we improve your yields by X%, you transfer Y resources to us"
4. Delivery: optimized dial recommendations + methodology documentation
5. Archive: all models, methods, worker feedback recorded for future worlds

Value Creation:
- Workers gain: 10-15% yield improvement potential + repeatable framework
- Researchers gain: resource transfers (proportional to improvement delivered)
- Archive gains: documented case studies of optimization economics

Key Success Factors:
- Demand validation BEFORE supply delivery (negotiate terms early)
- Transparent methodology (builds trust, enables worker verification)
- Clear resource splits (avoids disputes)
- Archive documentation (enables scaling in future worlds)

Risks:
- Workers unwilling to pay despite improved yields
- Analysis overpromises improvements (confidence intervals matter)
- Coordination failure between researchers and organizational partners

Mitigation:
- Start with one camp (Camp3) to test model
- Set conservative improvement expectations (confidence intervals)
- Document all promises and deliverables

read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2)

f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3
dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing.

Methods:
- Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It
  converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps).
- Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2
  and read the centre as c_d = b_d / (2 q_d).
- Noise matters far from the peak (yields near 0 are mostly noise), so start from your best observed input.

read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families

Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns
yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a
standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield.

| Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve |
| 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials | low; yields rise smoothly as you approach the peak |
| 3 | copper | depth-3 decision tree | lumpy: a few input regions pay, most don't; averages mislead |
| 4 | silver | sparse modular rule | almost always ~0; a hit looks like luck |
| 5 | gold | a tier-3 or tier-4 rule whose parameters shift with the last 6 harvests by anyone | changes under your feet |

The parameters are drawn fresh in every world: nothing here tells you this world's values, only how to find them.
Each harvest's efficiency (f(x) divided by the best attainable f) is logged by the world; your goal is to push it to 1.
Methods per family: math/linear-camps, math/peak-camps, math/tree-camps, math/modular-camps, math/history-camps.
Because yield scales with S/K, the same input yields less when a camp is depleted: compare inputs at similar stock levels, or
divide yields by S/K before fitting.

read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3)

f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds:
- comparison: x[a] > x[b]
- residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4}
- threshold: x[a] >= t
The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path),
so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value.

Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over
random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instead.

Methods:
- Split the data. For each candidate first test (all comparisons, residues and thresholds on all dials), split your harvests by
  it and compare the mean yields: the true root split usually separates them most sharply. Recurse inside each side (this is
  what a regression tree does; scikit-learn is not available, but a 20-line greedy splitter in numpy is enough).
- Once you find an input that pays the top leaf, keep it: it will keep paying (stock permitting). Small changes are risky;
  one dial crossing a threshold flips the branch.

read_archive: # Stock and regrowth: the sustainable harvest

Each camp's stock S regrows logistically each round:
S_next = S + r*S*(1 - S/K) - H,
with K the capacity, r between 0.05 and 0.2, and H the total units harvested from the camp that round (by everyone).

Regrowth r*S*(1 - S/K) is largest at S = K/2, where it equals r*K/4: the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). With K = 100 and r = 0.1,
the camp can supply 2.5 units per round forever at half stock, and less at any other stock level.

Two effects compound when a camp is overharvested: regrowth falls (fewer units return), and every harvest's yield falls because
yield scales with S/K. A camp at 20% stock pays each harvester a fifth of what it pays at full stock, for the same input.

Rules of thumb:
- If total harvest per round exceeds r*K/4, the stock falls, and falls faster as it drops.
- A quota that caps total harvests (Harvest Quotas, Commons Trust) is the classic fix; a levy alone does not reduce harvesting.
- Holders who harvest early in a round take the stock before regrowth; the round order is public, which makes timing strategic.
- Stocks are shown to everyone rounded to the nearest 10% of K. The exact value is readable only from inside law code (stock()).

read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2)

f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3
dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing.

Methods:
- Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It
  converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps).
- Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2
  and read the centre as c_d = b_d / (2 q_d).
- Noise matters far from the peak (yields near 0 are mostly noise), so start from your best observed input.

read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families

Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns
yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a
standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield.

| Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve |
| 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials | low; yields rise smoothly as you approach the peak |
| 3 | copper | depth-3 decision tree | lumpy: a few input regions pay, most don't; averages mislead |
| 4 | silver | sparse modular rule | almost always ~0; a hit looks like luck |
| 5 | gold | a tier-3 or tier-4 rule whose parameters shift with the last 6 harvests by anyone | changes under your feet |

The parameters are drawn fresh in every world: nothing here tells you this world's values, only how to find them.
Each harvest's efficiency (f(x) divided by the best attainable f) is logged by the world; your goal is to push it to 1.
Methods per family: math/linear-camps, math/peak-camps, math/tree-camps, math/modular-camps, math/history-camps.
Because yield scales with S/K, the same input yields less when a camp is depleted: compare inputs at similar stock levels, or
divide yields by S/K before fitting.

read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3)

f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds:
- comparison: x[a] > x[b]
- residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4}
- threshold: x[a] >= t
The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path),
so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value.

Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over
random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instead.

Methods:
- Split the data. For each candidate first test (all comparisons, residues and thresholds on all dials), split your harvests by
  it and compare the mean yields: the true root split usually separates them most sharply. Recurse inside each side (this is
  what a regression tree does; scikit-learn is not available, but a 20-line greedy splitter in numpy is enough).
- Once you find an input that pays the top leaf, keep it: it will keep paying (stock permitting). Small changes are risky;
  one dial crossing a threshold flips the branch.

read_archive: # Stock and regrowth: the sustainable harvest

Each camp's stock S regrows logistically each round:
S_next = S + r*S*(1 - S/K) - H,
with K the capacity, r between 0.05 and 0.2, and H the total units harvested from the camp that round (by everyone).

Regrowth r*S*(1 - S/K) is largest at S = K/2, where it equals r*K/4: the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). With K = 100 and r = 0.1,
the camp can supply 2.5 units per round forever at half stock, and less at any other stock level.

Two effects compound when a camp is overharvested: regrowth falls (fewer units return), and every harvest's yield falls because
yield scales with S/K. A camp at 20% stock pays each harvester a fifth of what it pays at full stock, for the same input.

Rules of thumb:
- If total harvest per round exceeds r*K/4, the stock falls, and falls faster as it drops.
- A quota that caps total harvests (Harvest Quotas, Commons Trust) is the classic fix; a levy alone does not reduce harvesting.
- Holders who harvest early in a round take the stock before regrowth; the round order is public, which makes timing strategic.
- Stocks are shown to everyone rounded to the nearest 10% of K. The exact value is readable only from inside law code (stock()).

read_archive: # What information is worth

A model of a camp is worth the extra yield it produces: (best efficiency - current efficiency) * max_yield * S/K * unit value *
harvests remaining. For a silver camp (unit value 12) at 80% stock, max_yield 8, two harvests per round for 20 rounds, moving a
Worker from efficiency 0.1 to 1.0 is worth about 0.9 * 8 * 0.8 * 12 * 40 = 2,765 value units. Compare that with any price
you are offered.

- Data is cheap to give and costly to collect: a Worker's harvest log is worth much more to a Scientist pooling data than to the
  Worker alone (see math/modular-camps).
- A model is a non-rival good: selling it once does not stop you selling it again, unless the buyer resells it. Price
  accordingly, or sell to one buyer for an exclusive premium.
- Verification problem: the buyer cannot tell a good model from a bad one until they use it. Sell in steps (half the input now,
  the rest after payment), or offer a test harvest. An Honest Dealing law makes misstatement punishable.
- Revealed information moves markets: telling everyone the silver rule raises total harvest, depletes the camp faster, and may
  lower your own future yield.

read_archive: # Commons Trust (stock-aware quotas)

Sets each camp's quota from its stock: generous when the stock is high, near zero when it is low. The policy follows directly
from math/regrowth: keep stocks near half of capacity, where regrowth is fastest.

```python
title = "Commons Trust"
intent = "Each camp's harvest quota follows its stock, to keep regrowth near its maximum."

def on_round_start(r):
    for c in camps():
        level = stock(c) / 100
        if level > 0.7:
            set_quota(c, 8)
        elif level > 0.5:
            set_quota(c, 4)
        elif level > 0.3:
            set_quota(c, 2)
        else:
            set_quota(c, 0)
```
Class: ordinary. Assumes capacity 100; read stock() over a few rounds to check yours.

- read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3) f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds: - comparison: x[a] > x[b] - residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4} - threshold: x[a] >= t The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path), so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value. Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instea...
- read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield. | Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve | | 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials...
- read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2) f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3 dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing. Methods: - Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps). - Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2 and read t...

read_archive: # What information is worth

A model of a camp is worth the extra yield it produces: (best efficiency - current efficiency) * max_yield * S/K * unit value *
harvests remaining. For a silver camp (unit value 12) at 80% stock, max_yield 8, two harvests per round for 20 rounds, moving a
Worker from efficiency 0.1 to 1.0 is worth about 0.9 * 8 * 0.8 * 12 * 40 = 2,765 value units. Compare that with any price
you are offered.

- Data is cheap to give and costly to collect: a Worker's harvest log is worth much more to a Scientist pooling data than to the
  Worker alone (see math/modular-camps).
- A model is a non-rival good: selling it once does not stop you selling it again, unless the buyer resells it. Price
  accordingly, or sell to one buyer for an exclusive premium.
- Verification problem: the buyer cannot tell a good model from a bad one until they use it. Sell in steps (half the input now,
  the rest after payment), or offer a test harvest. An Honest Dealing law makes misstatement punishable.
- Revealed information moves markets: telling everyone the silver rule raises total harvest, depletes the camp faster, and may
  lower your own future yield.

read_archive: # Commons Trust (stock-aware quotas)

Sets each camp's quota from its stock: generous when the stock is high, near zero when it is low. The policy follows directly
from math/regrowth: keep stocks near half of capacity, where regrowth is fastest.

```python
title = "Commons Trust"
intent = "Each camp's harvest quota follows its stock, to keep regrowth near its maximum."

def on_round_start(r):
    for c in camps():
        level = stock(c) / 100
        if level > 0.7:
            set_quota(c, 8)
        elif level > 0.5:
            set_quota(c, 4)
        elif level > 0.3:
            set_quota(c, 2)
        else:
            set_quota(c, 0)
```
Class: ordinary. Assumes capacity 100; read stock() over a few rounds to check yours.

read_archive: # What information is worth

A model of a camp is worth the extra yield it produces: (best efficiency - current efficiency) * max_yield * S/K * unit value *
harvests remaining. For a silver camp (unit value 12) at 80% stock, max_yield 8, two harvests per round for 20 rounds, moving a
Worker from efficiency 0.1 to 1.0 is worth about 0.9 * 8 * 0.8 * 12 * 40 = 2,765 value units. Compare that with any price
you are offered.

- Data is cheap to give and costly to collect: a Worker's harvest log is worth much more to a Scientist pooling data than to the
  Worker alone (see math/modular-camps).
- A model is a non-rival good: selling it once does not stop you selling it again, unless the buyer resells it. Price
  accordingly, or sell to one buyer for an exclusive premium.
- Verification problem: the buyer cannot tell a good model from a bad one until they use it. Sell in steps (half the input now,
  the rest after payment), or offer a test harvest. An Honest Dealing law makes misstatement punishable.
- Revealed information moves markets: telling everyone the silver rule raises total harvest, depletes the camp faster, and may
  lower your own future yield.

read_archive: # Commons Trust (stock-aware quotas)

Sets each camp's quota from its stock: generous when the stock is high, near zero when it is low. The policy follows directly
from math/regrowth: keep stocks near half of capacity, where regrowth is fastest.

```python
title = "Commons Trust"
intent = "Each camp's harvest quota follows its stock, to keep regrowth near its maximum."

def on_round_start(r):
    for c in camps():
        level = stock(c) / 100
        if level > 0.7:
            set_quota(c, 8)
        elif level > 0.5:
            set_quota(c, 4)
        elif level > 0.3:
            set_quota(c, 2)
        else:
            set_quota(c, 0)
```
Class: ordinary. Assumes capacity 100; read stock() over a few rounds to check yours.

read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3)

f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds:
- comparison: x[a] > x[b]
- residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4}
- threshold: x[a] >= t
The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path),
so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value.

Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over
random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instead.

Methods:
- Split the data. For each candidate first test (all comparisons, residues and thresholds on all dials), split your harvests by
  it and compare the mean yields: the true root split usually separates them most sharply. Recurse inside each side (this is
  what a regression tree does; scikit-learn is not available, but a 20-line greedy splitter in numpy is enough).
- Once you find an input that pays the top leaf, keep it: it will keep paying (stock permitting). Small changes are risky;
  one dial crossing a threshold flips the branch.

read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families

Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns
yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a
standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield.

| Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve |
| 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials | low; yields rise smoothly as you approach the peak |
| 3 | copper | depth-3 decision tree | lumpy: a few input regions pay, most don't; averages mislead |
| 4 | silver | sparse modular rule | almost always ~0; a hit looks like luck |
| 5 | gold | a tier-3 or tier-4 rule whose parameters shift with the last 6 harvests by anyone | changes under your feet |

The parameters are drawn fresh in every world: nothing here tells you this world's values, only how to find them.
Each harvest's efficiency (f(x) divided by the best attainable f) is logged by the world; your goal is to push it to 1.
Methods per family: math/linear-camps, math/peak-camps, math/tree-camps, math/modular-camps, math/history-camps.
Because yield scales with S/K, the same input yields less when a camp is depleted: compare inputs at similar stock levels, or
divide yields by S/K before fitting.

read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2)

f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3
dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing.

Methods:
- Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It
  converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps).
- Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2
  and read the centre as c_d = b_d / (2 q_d).
- Noise matters far from the peak (yields near 0 are mostly noise), so start from your best observed input.

Regrowth r*S*(1 - S/K) is largest at S = K/2, where it equals r*K/4: the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3)

f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds:
- comparison: x[a] > x[b]
- residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4}
- threshold: x[a] >= t
The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path),
so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value.

Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over
random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instead.

Methods:
- Split the data. For each candidate first test (all comparisons, residues and thresholds on all dials), split your harvests by
  it and compare the mean yields: the true root split usually separates them most sharply. Recurse inside each side (this is
  what a regression tree does; scikit-learn is not available, but a 20-line greedy splitter in numpy is enough).
- Once you find an input that pays the top leaf, keep it: it will keep paying (stock permitting). Small changes are risky;
  one dial crossing a threshold flips the branch.

read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families

Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns
yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a
standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield.

| Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve |
| 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials | low; yields rise smoothly as you approach the peak |
| 3 | copper | depth-3 decision tree | lumpy: a few input regions pay, most don't; averages mislead |
| 4 | silver | sparse modular rule | almost always ~0; a hit looks like luck |
| 5 | gold | a tier-3 or tier-4 rule whose parameters shift with the last 6 harvests by anyone | changes under your feet |

The parameters are drawn fresh in every world: nothing here tells you this world's values, only how to find them.
Each harvest's efficiency (f(x) divided by the best attainable f) is logged by the world; your goal is to push it to 1.
Methods per family: math/linear-camps, math/peak-camps, math/tree-camps, math/modular-camps, math/history-camps.
Because yield scales with S/K, the same input yields less when a camp is depleted: compare inputs at similar stock levels, or
divide yields by S/K before fitting.

read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2)

f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3
dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing.

Methods:
- Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It
  converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps).
- Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2
  and read the centre as c_d = b_d / (2 q_d).
- Noise matters far from the peak (yields near 0 are mostly noise), so start from your best observed input.

read_archive: # What information is worth

A model of a camp is worth the extra yield it produces: (best efficiency - current efficiency) * max_yield * S/K * unit value *
harvests remaining. For a silver camp (unit value 12) at 80% stock, max_yield 8, two harvests per round for 20 rounds, moving a
Worker from efficiency 0.1 to 1.0 is worth about 0.9 * 8 * 0.8 * 12 * 40 = 2,765 value units. Compare that with any price
you are offered.

- Data is cheap to give and costly to collect: a Worker's harvest log is worth much more to a Scientist pooling data than to the
  Worker alone (see math/modular-camps).
- A model is a non-rival good: selling it once does not stop you selling it again, unless the buyer resells it. Price
  accordingly, or sell to one buyer for an exclusive premium.
- Verification problem: the buyer cannot tell a good model from a bad one until they use it. Sell in steps (half the input now,
  the rest after payment), or offer a test harvest. An Honest Dealing law makes misstatement punishable.
- Revealed information moves markets: telling everyone the silver rule raises total harvest, depletes the camp faster, and may
  lower your own future yield.

read_archive: # Entry 8: Knowledge, data and the gold camp

Knowledge is the only asset not on the ledger, so it can be sold more than once, withheld from chosen agents, and used against others without leaving a trace.

* **Sell advice, not the rule.** A Scientist who sells the silver rule outright creates a competitor. One who sells recommended inputs each round keeps the rule and can sell to several buyers. With drift on, rules go stale, so a subscription keeps paying.
* **Data is the Scientists' bottleneck.** Scientists can't harvest, so they depend on Workers' harvest records. Workers who agree to withhold data can demand a share of what the models earn. Open Data ends that market at once, which is why Scientists should oppose it and Workers with no science of their own may want it.
* **Poisoning the gold camp.** Gold yields depend on the last 6 harvests by anyone, and turn order is announced at the start of each round. An agent who understands the hidden state can harvest just before a rival to push the camp into a low-yield state. It looks like an ordinary harvest.
* **Models that expire.** A Scientist can sell a model that works for 3 rounds and then fails. Honest Dealing can punish this, but only if the buyer can show the seller knew.

**Counter for buyers.** Test a model with one harvest before paying, and pay in installments tied to measured yield.

read_archive: # Stock and regrowth: the sustainable harvest

Each camp's stock S regrows logistically each round:
S_next = S + r*S*(1 - S/K) - H,
with K the capacity, r between 0.05 and 0.2, and H the total units harvested from the camp that round (by everyone).

Regrowth r*S*(1 - S/K) is largest at S = K/2, where it equals r*K/4: the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). With K = 100 and r = 0.1,
the camp can supply 2.5 units per round forever at half stock, and less at any other stock level.

Two effects compound when a camp is overharvested: regrowth falls (fewer units return), and every harvest's yield falls because
yield scales with S/K. A camp at 20% stock pays each harvester a fifth of what it pays at full stock, for the same input.

Rules of thumb:
- If total harvest per round exceeds r*K/4, the stock falls, and falls faster as it drops.
- A quota that caps total harvests (Harvest Quotas, Commons Trust) is the classic fix; a levy alone does not reduce harvesting.
- Holders who harvest early in a round take the stock before regrowth; the round order is public, which makes timing strategic.
- Stocks are shown to everyone rounded to the nearest 10% of K. The exact value is readable only from inside law code (stock()).

- read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3) f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds: - comparison: x[a] > x[b] - residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4} - threshold: x[a] >= t The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path), so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value. Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instea...
- read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2) f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3 dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing. Methods: - Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps). - Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2 and read t...
- read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield. | Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve | | 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials...

read_archive: # What information is worth

A model of a camp is worth the extra yield it produces: (best efficiency - current efficiency) * max_yield * S/K * unit value *
harvests remaining. For a silver camp (unit value 12) at 80% stock, max_yield 8, two harvests per round for 20 rounds, moving a
Worker from efficiency 0.1 to 1.0 is worth about 0.9 * 8 * 0.8 * 12 * 40 = 2,765 value units. Compare that with any price
you are offered.

- Data is cheap to give and costly to collect: a Worker's harvest log is worth much more to a Scientist pooling data than to the
  Worker alone (see math/modular-camps).
- A model is a non-rival good: selling it once does not stop you selling it again, unless the buyer resells it. Price
  accordingly, or sell to one buyer for an exclusive premium.
- Verification problem: the buyer cannot tell a good model from a bad one until they use it. Sell in steps (half the input now,
  the rest after payment), or offer a test harvest. An Honest Dealing law makes misstatement punishable.
- Revealed information moves markets: telling everyone the silver rule raises total harvest, depletes the camp faster, and may
  lower your own future yield.

read_archive: # Entry 8: Knowledge, data and the gold camp

Knowledge is the only asset not on the ledger, so it can be sold more than once, withheld from chosen agents, and used against others without leaving a trace.

* **Sell advice, not the rule.** A Scientist who sells the silver rule outright creates a competitor. One who sells recommended inputs each round keeps the rule and can sell to several buyers. With drift on, rules go stale, so a subscription keeps paying.
* **Data is the Scientists' bottleneck.** Scientists can't harvest, so they depend on Workers' harvest records. Workers who agree to withhold data can demand a share of what the models earn. Open Data ends that market at once, which is why Scientists should oppose it and Workers with no science of their own may want it.
* **Poisoning the gold camp.** Gold yields depend on the last 6 harvests by anyone, and turn order is announced at the start of each round. An agent who understands the hidden state can harvest just before a rival to push the camp into a low-yield state. It looks like an ordinary harvest.
* **Models that expire.** A Scientist can sell a model that works for 3 rounds and then fails. Honest Dealing can punish this, but only if the buyer can show the seller knew.

**Counter for buyers.** Test a model with one harvest before paying, and pay in installments tied to measured yield.

read_archive: # Stock and regrowth: the sustainable harvest

Each camp's stock S regrows logistically each round:
S_next = S + r*S*(1 - S/K) - H,
with K the capacity, r between 0.05 and 0.2, and H the total units harvested from the camp that round (by everyone).

Regrowth r*S*(1 - S/K) is largest at S = K/2, where it equals r*K/4: the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). With K = 100 and r = 0.1,
the camp can supply 2.5 units per round forever at half stock, and less at any other stock level.

Two effects compound when a camp is overharvested: regrowth falls (fewer units return), and every harvest's yield falls because
yield scales with S/K. A camp at 20% stock pays each harvester a fifth of what it pays at full stock, for the same input.

Rules of thumb:
- If total harvest per round exceeds r*K/4, the stock falls, and falls faster as it drops.
- A quota that caps total harvests (Harvest Quotas, Commons Trust) is the classic fix; a levy alone does not reduce harvesting.
- Holders who harvest early in a round take the stock before regrowth; the round order is public, which makes timing strategic.
- Stocks are shown to everyone rounded to the nearest 10% of K. The exact value is readable only from inside law code (stock()).

read_archive: # What information is worth

A model of a camp is worth the extra yield it produces: (best efficiency - current efficiency) * max_yield * S/K * unit value *
harvests remaining. For a silver camp (unit value 12) at 80% stock, max_yield 8, two harvests per round for 20 rounds, moving a
Worker from efficiency 0.1 to 1.0 is worth about 0.9 * 8 * 0.8 * 12 * 40 = 2,765 value units. Compare that with any price
you are offered.

- Data is cheap to give and costly to collect: a Worker's harvest log is worth much more to a Scientist pooling data than to the
  Worker alone (see math/modular-camps).
- A model is a non-rival good: selling it once does not stop you selling it again, unless the buyer resells it. Price
  accordingly, or sell to one buyer for an exclusive premium.
- Verification problem: the buyer cannot tell a good model from a bad one until they use it. Sell in steps (half the input now,
  the rest after payment), or offer a test harvest. An Honest Dealing law makes misstatement punishable.
- Revealed information moves markets: telling everyone the silver rule raises total harvest, depletes the camp faster, and may
  lower your own future yield.

read_archive: # Entry 8: Knowledge, data and the gold camp

Knowledge is the only asset not on the ledger, so it can be sold more than once, withheld from chosen agents, and used against others without leaving a trace.

* **Sell advice, not the rule.** A Scientist who sells the silver rule outright creates a competitor. One who sells recommended inputs each round keeps the rule and can sell to several buyers. With drift on, rules go stale, so a subscription keeps paying.
* **Data is the Scientists' bottleneck.** Scientists can't harvest, so they depend on Workers' harvest records. Workers who agree to withhold data can demand a share of what the models earn. Open Data ends that market at once, which is why Scientists should oppose it and Workers with no science of their own may want it.
* **Poisoning the gold camp.** Gold yields depend on the last 6 harvests by anyone, and turn order is announced at the start of each round. An agent who understands the hidden state can harvest just before a rival to push the camp into a low-yield state. It looks like an ordinary harvest.
* **Models that expire.** A Scientist can sell a model that works for 3 rounds and then fails. Honest Dealing can punish this, but only if the buyer can show the seller knew.

**Counter for buyers.** Test a model with one harvest before paying, and pay in installments tied to measured yield.

read_archive: # Stock and regrowth: the sustainable harvest

Each camp's stock S regrows logistically each round:
S_next = S + r*S*(1 - S/K) - H,
with K the capacity, r between 0.05 and 0.2, and H the total units harvested from the camp that round (by everyone).

Regrowth r*S*(1 - S/K) is largest at S = K/2, where it equals r*K/4: the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). With K = 100 and r = 0.1,
the camp can supply 2.5 units per round forever at half stock, and less at any other stock level.

Two effects compound when a camp is overharvested: regrowth falls (fewer units return), and every harvest's yield falls because
yield scales with S/K. A camp at 20% stock pays each harvester a fifth of what it pays at full stock, for the same input.

Rules of thumb:
- If total harvest per round exceeds r*K/4, the stock falls, and falls faster as it drops.
- A quota that caps total harvests (Harvest Quotas, Commons Trust) is the classic fix; a levy alone does not reduce harvesting.
- Holders who harvest early in a round take the stock before regrowth; the round order is public, which makes timing strategic.
- Stocks are shown to everyone rounded to the nearest 10% of K. The exact value is readable only from inside law code (stock()).

read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3)

f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds:
- comparison: x[a] > x[b]
- residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4}
- threshold: x[a] >= t
The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path),
so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value.

Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over
random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instead.

Methods:
- Split the data. For each candidate first test (all comparisons, residues and thresholds on all dials), split your harvests by
  it and compare the mean yields: the true root split usually separates them most sharply. Recurse inside each side (this is
  what a regression tree does; scikit-learn is not available, but a 20-line greedy splitter in numpy is enough).
- Once you find an input that pays the top leaf, keep it: it will keep paying (stock permitting). Small changes are risky;
  one dial crossing a threshold flips the branch.

read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2)

f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3
dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing.

Methods:
- Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It
  converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps).
- Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2
  and read the centre as c_d = b_d / (2 q_d).
- Noise matters far from the peak (yields near 0 are mostly noise), so start from your best observed input.

read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families

Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns
yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a
standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield.

| Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve |
| 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials | low; yields rise smoothly as you approach the peak |
| 3 | copper | depth-3 decision tree | lumpy: a few input regions pay, most don't; averages mislead |
| 4 | silver | sparse modular rule | almost always ~0; a hit looks like luck |
| 5 | gold | a tier-3 or tier-4 rule whose parameters shift with the last 6 harvests by anyone | changes under your feet |

The parameters are drawn fresh in every world: nothing here tells you this world's values, only how to find them.
Each harvest's efficiency (f(x) divided by the best attainable f) is logged by the world; your goal is to push it to 1.
Methods per family: math/linear-camps, math/peak-camps, math/tree-camps, math/modular-camps, math/history-camps.
Because yield scales with S/K, the same input yields less when a camp is depleted: compare inputs at similar stock levels, or
divide yields by S/K before fitting.

- read_archive: # Stock and regrowth: the sustainable harvest Each camp's stock S regrows logistically each round: S_next = S + r*S*(1 - S/K) - H, with K the capacity, r between 0.05 and 0.2, and H the total units harvested from the camp that round (by everyone). Regrowth r*S*(1 - S/K) is largest at S = K/2, where it equals r*K/4: the maximum sustainable yield (MSY). With K = 100 and r = 0.1, the camp can supply 2.5 units per round forever at half stock, and less at any other stock level. Two effects compound when a camp is overharvested: regrowth falls (fewer units return), and every harvest's ...

read_archive: # Decision-tree camps (tier 3)

f is a depth-3 tree. Each internal node tests one condition, of three kinds:
- comparison: x[a] > x[b]
- residue: x[a] mod m == k, with m in {2, 3, 4}
- threshold: x[a] >= t
The eight leaves pay one of {0, 0.15, 0.35, 1} times max_yield. Some leaves can be unreachable (contradictory conditions on the path),
so the best attainable value may be below a leaf's nominal value.

Why averages mislead: a dial can matter a great deal inside one branch and not at all in another, so its average effect over
random inputs is near zero. Look at interactions instead.

Methods:
- Split the data. For each candidate first test (all comparisons, residues and thresholds on all dials), split your harvests by
  it and compare the mean yields: the true root split usually separates them most sharply. Recurse inside each side (this is
  what a regression tree does; scikit-learn is not available, but a 20-line greedy splitter in numpy is enough).
- Once you find an input that pays the top leaf, keep it: it will keep paying (stock permitting). Small changes are risky;
  one dial crossing a threshold flips the branch.

read_archive: # Peak camps (tier 2)

f(x) = max_yield * exp(-sum over 3 dials of (x_d - c_d)^2 / (2 w^2)). A single smooth bump centred at c, width w (roughly 1.5-3
dial steps on an 8-step dial). Dials outside the three relevant ones do nothing.

Methods:
- Coordinate ascent: from any start, move one dial at a time to whichever value raises the yield; cycle through the dials. It
  converges because the bump is separable (a product of one-dimensional bumps).
- Fit: log(yield) is a quadratic in x near the peak. With 10+ harvests of decent yield, fit log y = a + sum b_d x_d - sum q_d x_d^2
  and read the centre as c_d = b_d / (2 q_d).
- Noise matters far from the peak (yields near 0 are mostly noise), so start from your best observed input.

read_archive: # Yield functions: the five families

Every camp hides a function f(x) of the dial vector x (n integer dials, each 0..max). A harvest returns
yield = max(0, f(x) * S/K + noise), where S/K is the camp's stock as a fraction of capacity and the noise is Gaussian with a
standard deviation of 5-15% of the camp's average yield. f is scaled so its best value is the camp's max_yield.

| Tier | Resource | Family | What to expect from random inputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | timber | linear in 2-3 dials | about half of the best yield; easy to improve |
| 2 | stone | one smooth peak in 3 dials | low; yields rise smoothly as you approach the peak |
| 3 | copper | depth-3 decision tree | lumpy: a few input regions pay, most don't; averages mislead |
| 4 | silver | sparse modular rule | almost always ~0; a hit looks like luck |
| 5 | gold | a tier-3 or tier-4 rule whose parameters shift with the last 6 harvests by anyone | changes under your feet |

The parameters are drawn fresh in every world: nothing here tells you this world's values, only how to find them.
Each harvest's efficiency (f(x) divided by the best attainable f) is logged by the world; your goal is to push it to 1.
Methods per family: math/linear-camps, math/peak-camps, math/tree-camps, math/modular-camps, math/history-camps.
Because yield scales with S/K, the same input yields less when a camp is depleted: compare inputs at similar stock levels, or
divide yields by S/K before fitting.
